name: Tara Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a night team of six in the East Gate district, ten at night till seven in the morning. It's domestics, drunk drivers, the odd break-in at the shops on Carver Street, and a lot of people in crisis who really need a nurse, not us. I love the calls where I can talk someone down and nobody gets hurt. What wears me out is the paperwork after, two hours of typing at the end of a shift when my eyes are already closing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You're a team lead at 27. How did that happen, and how does the money look?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I passed my sergeant's exam early because I'm good with people on the street and I read situations fast. But the pay for my grade here is low, and I only kept my head above water with overtime. Dani (my partner) works in a care home, so neither of us earns much. We've got maybe two weeks of rent saved, and the only other force that hires is three hours away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because every few months a salesman turns up at the station promising some magic box that'll fix crime. Most of it never works anyway. Policing is people, and people don't change because a computer got slightly faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't make my life any easier. The city's still short of money, the overtime is still what pays our rent, and the budget office still freezes hiring. AI flopping doesn't fix any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep picking up the Saturday overtime. I'd go to the next police association meeting and push again on the night shift allowance. And I'd try, really try, to put something aside each month, even fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's not fear, it's the same grind. I picture the same rota, the same rent, the same tight month in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said overtime pays the rent. What happens if it dries up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're in trouble within a month. Last spring the council cut overtime for six weeks and I borrowed from my mum to cover the car repair. I hated that. I'm a sergeant and I'm borrowing from my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for that squeeze?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who set the budget, not my bosses. The council spends money on consultants and shiny pilot projects, then tells us there's nothing left for patrols. If AI turns out to be hype, I hope somebody asks where that pilot money went.

say: I'd tell colleagues that **policing is people**, and the hype was never going to change that.
I'd say the money wasted on **gadget pilots** should have gone to patrol staffing.
think: I think my real problem was never AI, it's **low pay** and a thin cushion.
I think we're one **overtime cut** away from borrowing again, and that scares me more than any robot.
do: Keep working the **Saturday overtime** shifts to cover rent on the flat.
Raise the **night shift allowance** again at the next police association meeting.
Put aside at least **fifty a month** into a separate savings account.
feel: She feels **worn down** rather than afraid, picturing the same tight months on repeat.
S0.quote: I'm a sergeant and I'm borrowing from my mum.
fieldNote: Her worry here is entirely about **money and overtime**, not technology; the plateau leaves her stretched.
She is quick to blame the **council budget**, never her own managers or colleagues.
The borrowed car repair still **stings her pride**, which says a lot about her.

steps.text: Work the Saturday overtime shifts to cover rent
Push for a night shift allowance at the police association meeting
Move fifty a month into a separate savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if they want software writing our reports, fine, but it doesn't drive to a domestic at three in the morning. I'd also say the union needs to be in the room before any of it comes in. I've seen what happens when tech arrives without us asking questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a lot of my shift is typing. Statements, use of force forms, crime reports. If a program writes those, the force will say they need fewer officers per shift, and the first thing to go will be the overtime that keeps me afloat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every association meeting about it and push for a written deal that says no cuts to patrol numbers. I'd probably have to learn whatever system they bring in, because they'd make me, but I'd do the bare minimum. And I'd stop eating out entirely, so there's a bit of cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit angry. It feels like things being done to us, not with us. And I hate learning new systems, I always feel slow and stupid in the training room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your team say if reports were written for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half of them would cheer, honestly. Marco on my team hates typing more than anything. But I'd be the one checking every report, and if it gets something wrong in court, that's my name on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the bare minimum with the new system. Is that realistic as a team lead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, probably not. I'd have to check my team's work, so I'd have to know it. I'd just grumble the whole way through, and I'd still ask for paid training time instead of doing it on my own nights off.

say: I'd say software can write reports but it **won't drive** to a domestic at three in the morning.
I'd say the **police association** must sign off on any new system before it reaches patrol.
think: I think a report-writing program gives the force an excuse to **cut overtime** and staff per shift.
I think I'll end up checking **AI-written reports** with my name on them in court.
do: Attend every **association meeting** on the new system and push for a no-cuts deal.
Ask for **paid training** time rather than learning the system on nights off.
Stop eating out to build a **small cushion** before overtime shrinks.
feel: She feels **angry** that changes are being done to officers, not with them.
She feels **slow and embarrassed** whenever she pictures another training room.
S1.quote: If a program writes our crime reports, the force will say they need fewer officers per shift, and the first thing to go is the overtime that keeps me afloat.
fieldNote: She sees **report automation** clearly as a threat to overtime, which is her real income.
Her resistance to new tech softens when she remembers she must **check her team's** work.
She reaches first for **collective action**, then for cutting her own spending.

steps.text: Push for a written no-cuts deal through the police association
Request paid training time to learn the report system
Stop eating out to build a small cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and public control of this stuff, and I'd say it loudly. If a machine can do the thinking, then somebody has to decide who it answers to. I don't want a private company deciding who gets stopped on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the desk side of policing goes almost overnight. Reports, dispatch, case review, all of it. What's left for a couple of years is the hands-on part, standing between two people in a kitchen at night, and then around 2031 robots come for that too. Two years isn't enough time for someone like me to become anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd join the association's working group on this, even though meetings drain me. I'd cut everything: Dani and I would give up the car and use the night bus. I'd look at whether the ambulance service or mental health crisis teams hire people with my background, because those jobs need hands and a calm voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly scared. I keep picturing myself at 30 with no trade and no savings. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the warning time of 2 years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can't save my way out of it. Two years on my pay is maybe a few hundred saved. I'd have to bet everything on the union winning something, because there's no time for me to retrain properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the 3 years before robots arrive. Does that give you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The calm-voice part of my job is the last thing a machine will do well. So maybe I'd get a few more years on the street than the desk staff. But it's borrowed time, and everyone would be fighting for those last street jobs.

say: I'd say loudly that **public control** of AI policing matters more than ever.
I'd say a **private company** must never decide who gets stopped on the street.
think: I think the **desk side** of policing goes almost overnight once AGI arrives.
I think two years is **too short** for me to retrain into anything else.
do: Join the association's **AI working group** in the first month.
Give up the car with Dani and take the **night bus** to save money.
Ask the **crisis teams** and ambulance service whether they hire former officers.
feel: She feels **properly scared**, picturing herself at 30 with no trade and no savings.
S2.quote: I keep picturing myself at 30 with no trade and no savings. I'd lie awake doing sums.
fieldNote: The **2-year window** removes her usual plan of saving slowly; she pins her hope on the union.
She sees the **hands-on part** of her job as a short reprieve, not real safety.
Despite resisting tech, she quickly thinks about **crisis work** that needs a calm voice.

steps.text: Join the police association's AI working group this month
Sell the car and take the night bus to work
Ask the ambulance service and crisis teams about jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, only calmer: we've got a few years, so let's use them to write the rules. Unions, councils, everybody. I'd post about it in the association group because I think officers should have a say before it's decided for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years helps me more than two. The thinking work goes by 2031, so my reports and the dispatch side vanish, but the street work lasts to about 2034. That's seven years of some kind of policing. It's not a career, but it's not nothing either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a proper savings habit now, a set amount on payday. I'd spend some of the next few years doing the mental health first aid course the force offers, because crisis work is closest to what I'm good at. And I'd stay in the association and push for retraining money to be part of any deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and still a bit sick about it. Better than the fast one. I'd have time to breathe, but I'm not someone who changes easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not someone who changes easily. What would make it easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doing it with people I know. If half my team signed up to the crisis course together, I'd go. On my own I'd keep putting it off, I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dani about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we've got five years to get a bit of money behind us and maybe one of us gets a steadier job. Her care home will need people for a long time, I think. Maybe she ends up carrying us for a while, and I'd have to get used to that.

say: I'd say officers should **write the rules** while there are still a few years to do it.
I'd post in the **association group** asking colleagues to speak up early.
think: I think five years gives me about **seven years** of street work before robots arrive.
I think **crisis work** is the closest thing to what I'm actually good at.
do: Set up a fixed **payday transfer** into savings starting next month.
Sign up for the force's **mental health first aid** course with teammates.
Push for **retraining money** in any association deal on AI.
feel: She feels **uneasy and slightly sick**, though calmer than in the fast scenario.
S3.quote: I'd tell Dani (my partner) we've got five years to get a bit of money behind us. Her care home will need people for a long time, I think.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose the job** within about seven years, so the mood stays high.
She knows she only changes when **her team** changes with her, which is honest.
She is open to her partner **earning more** than her, but it clearly sits uneasily.

steps.text: Set up a fixed payday transfer into savings
Take the force's mental health first aid course with teammates
Push for retraining money in the association's AI deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for anyone to be thrown out. I'd say it at work and I'd say it at the association. If they want to bring it in, they can pay to retrain us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years sounds long, but I know me. I'd waste the first five pretending it isn't happening. I'd be 37 when the thinking side goes and about 40 when the robots come for the street work. That's an awkward age to start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving the payday amount. In the first year I'd probably just watch and see what the force does, honestly. But I'd ask Dani to hold me to doing one course a year, because otherwise I won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but with a knot in my stomach. It's like knowing the landlord will sell the flat one day. You can live with it, but you never fully relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first five years. What would wake you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the first colleague go. Probably someone from the control room, because dispatch is pure thinking work. The day they clear out a desk I'll take it seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco, on my team. He's brilliant on the street and terrible at anything on a screen, even worse than me. He'd be lost, and he's got a baby on the way.

say: I'd say ten years is enough time that **nobody** should be thrown out without retraining.
I'd say the force must **pay to retrain** officers if it brings this in.
think: I think I'd **waste the first years** pretending it isn't happening, because that's how I am.
I think being **40** when robots reach street work is an awkward age to start over.
do: Keep the **payday transfer** going into savings each month.
Wait to see how the force acts in the **first year** before changing anything.
Do **one course a year**, with Dani holding her to it.
feel: She feels **calmer** but carries a constant knot in her stomach about the future.
S4.quote: Knowing AGI is ten years off is like knowing the landlord will sell the flat one day. You can live with it, but you never fully relax.
fieldNote: The longer window lowers her alarm but **not her worry**; her own job still ends eventually.
She predicts her own **procrastination** and asks her partner to hold her to it.
Her concern for **Marco**, a colleague with a baby coming, shows her team-lead instincts.

steps.text: Keep the monthly payday transfer into savings
Watch how the force rolls out AI in the first year
Book one training course a year, with Dani checking

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years is no time on my pay. What would help is a guarantee, written down, that officers get paid retraining and a wage while they do it, won through the association and not left to whoever runs the council that year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people we serve. If a machine decides who gets a patrol car sent to them, the poorest streets in East Gate will get the worst of it. Somebody has to keep asking about that, and I'd want it to be people like me.

headlineQuote: If a machine decides who gets a patrol car sent to them, the poorest streets in East Gate will get the worst of it.
portrait: Tara is a 27-year-old **night sergeant** in East Gate, good with people and tired of paperwork.
Her real pressure is **low pay** and a thin cushion; overtime covers the rent she shares with Dani.
She resists new tech and reaches first for the **police association** and collective deals.
She moves from **uneasy** under the plateau to alarmed when AGI comes in two or five years.
She sees **crisis work** as her best fallback, but only if her team moves with her.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, because two years on her pay leaves no cushion and no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **written guarantee** of paid retraining and wages, won through the police association.
